rows.subtype: Child too shy or proud to ask [Actor]
rows.description: A schoolchild sits confused over a problem and says nothing, afraid of looking stupid in front of classmates. Silence feels safer than exposure, so confusion quietly grows.

A teenager struggles alone with a subject because asking a teacher feels like admitting failure, especially among peers who seem to understand. Pride and fear of judgment cost weeks of avoidable struggle.

rows.subtype: Waiting until it is too late [Actor]
rows.description: A student hides falling behind until an exam is near and only then asks for help. Shame delays the request, and delay makes the problem larger and the help harder to give.
A teenager hints "It is getting late" to suggest leaving or implies displeasure without saying it. Hints save face but are often missed, so clear requests avoid confusion.
A young professional reads "That might be difficult" or "We will try" as possible refusal in some settings and as a real maybe in others. Following up with a clear question reduces misreading.

rows.subtype: Playground story grows with each telling [Actor]
rows.description: A child hears from many classmates that the old tree is haunted and believes it more after each retelling; repetition makes an idea feel true and important.
A young adult forwards an alarming health or safety message because many others have; how often they see it is taken as proof, and doubters feel cold or careless.

rows.subtype: Controlling a frown at a parent or teacher [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager tries to smooth a frowning brow when disagreeing with an adult to avoid conflict, though the forehead may still tense. Naming the disagreement in words is clearer than relying on the face.
A young adult in an interview raises the brows to show interest and avoids furrowing them when nervous. Interviewers should remember that a tense forehead may only signal effort or anxiety.
A toddler told not to touch something reaches for it at once. Being restricted makes the forbidden thing more attractive and he asserts his own will.
A preschooler refuses help or an instruction just because it was ordered, then complies happily if given a choice between two acceptable options.
A teenager told firmly what to do or whom to avoid does the opposite, protecting his sense of freedom. Heavy pressure can make risky things more tempting.
A teenager may promise to keep a secret or a pledge of loyalty to a friend. Promises to keep secrets about safety, harm or abuse should not be kept, and telling a trusted adult is the caring choice.

A young adult may take vows in marriage, religion, or a profession, which carry cultural meaning and legal weight. The seriousness differs by culture, so a person asks what the commitment means to each side.
